tier_reason: docs/MEASUREMENTS.md 'The standardised run on ad7d338' has every cell quoted (own-format decode 18/18 cells +14% to +83%, LZ4-block decode 20/27 ahead, packing 25/27 ahead) against liblz4 in the same Criterion process; bench code is public (benches/codec.rs, required-features liblz4), the compiler is pinned (rust-toolchain.toml channel 1.85), flags are in Cargo.toml (release lto="fat", codegen-units=1), and CPUs are named (Xeon 8481C / EPYC 9B14 / Neoverse V2 on GCE c3/c3d/c4a-standard-4, Debian 12 with apt liblz4-dev per scripts/bench-on-gce.sh).

corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.85 (pinned in rust-toolchain.toml); Cargo release profile lto="fat", codegen-units=1, default opt-level 3; assembly kernels built through build.rs with the cc crate; Criterion 0.5 harness (benches/codec.rs); baseline liblz4 is the Debian 12 liblz4-dev apt package (scripts/bench-on-gce.sh), its version and build flags not stated in the log
corrections.hardware: Google Cloud c3-standard-4 (Intel Xeon 8481C), c3d-standard-4 (AMD EPYC 9B14), c4a-standard-4 (Google Axion, Neoverse V2), Debian 12 images; 4-vCPU shared cloud VMs; an Apple M2 Max appears only in a separate four-machine run
corrections.caveats: Brand-new single-author project with 0 stars (263 commits, extracted from the author's KevaVolt project); latest commit 2026-10-02 corrected a misattributed capacity x throughput table in the README (the M2 column had been dropped and labels shifted), which does not affect the decode/pack tables quoted here. The standardised run was on revision ad7d338, which does not exist in this repo's history (commit page 404), and scripts/bench-on-gce.sh still builds the monorepo package keva-core and calls scripts/packer-report.sh, which this repo does not ship, so reproduction needs `make bench` / benches/codec.rs instead. Throughput is counted against unpacked bytes, so smaller output inflates the number. Packing is not ahead on varied_4k Neoverse V2 (-2%) or varied_64k EPYC (+0%). Reading raw LZ4 blocks loses on 7 of 27 cells, worst noise_512 on x86 (-15% Xeon, -12% EPYC); the author attributes this to buffer-placement sensitivity. Rust with hand-written assembly; usable from C++ only through its C ABI (include/lzvolt.h, staticlib/cdylib); assembly kernels only on Linux/macOS x86-64 and aarch64, portable Rust elsewhere. Compared only against liblz4 and lz4_flex, not zstd or other fast LZ codecs.

notes: All numbers in claimed_speedup match the README and the MEASUREMENTS.md standardised run exactly; the 20/27 and 25/27 counts check out against the per-cell tables. The measurement log is unusually candid (records refuted ideas and losing cells), but the measured revision is not in the public history, which is worth an enricher look.

tier_reason: Benchmark code (benchmarks/report/run_report_benchmarks.py, benchmarks/core) and raw samples (benchmarks/results/2026-07-14/report-benchmarks.json) are public and the CPU is named (Xeon W-2235, WSL2 guest), but the C++ compiler and version for the CLI build are not stated in the README, the technical report PDF, or the archived metadata, so not A; the arXiv report is a first-party preprint, not peer review, so C.

corrections.baseline: pigz 2.6 (system zlib) and gzip (archived run metadata records gzip 1.10; the README table labels it gzip 1.12)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: C++23 via CMake Release build (README/report state the C++ core is Release -O3 for the Go/OCI benchmark); C++ compiler name and version not recorded in README, report/pigzpp-report.pdf or the archived metadata, which lists only rustc 1.93.0, go 1.22.5, node 22.16.0 and a conda Python built with GCC 14.3.0
corrections.hardware: Intel Xeon W-2235 host; Ubuntu 22.04 WSL2 guest (kernel 6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2) exposing 5 cores / 10 logical CPUs; median of 7 timed samples after 1 warm-up; affinity, turbo and frequency not controlled (per metadata timing_policy)
corrections.caveats: Very new, single-author C++23 rewrite of pigz (described by the author as an experiment in AI-agent-assisted modernization). Baseline pigz uses the system zlib, so much of the gain is zlib-ng and ISA-L (both already catalogued) rather than new compression code. gzip is single-threaded, so the 66x-vs-gzip figure is mostly parallelism. Benchmarks ran in a WSL2 guest on one CPU with one text corpus; the archived metadata marks the working tree as dirty (commit e7e3286, dirty=true) and records gzip 1.10 while the README says gzip 1.12. The 8.5x figure trades about 9% more output (ratio 2.58 vs 2.83). Compiler name/version for the CLI run not stated. The technical report (arXiv 2608.24153, also checked in as report/pigzpp-report.pdf) is a first-party preprint.

notes: All CLI and decompression numbers match the README, the checked-in report PDF and the raw JSON (gzip 16.6, pigz 132.9, pigzpp zlib 284.6, isal 1124.4 MB/s; decompress 165.5/212.1/711.4 MB/s). Downgraded A to C only because the C++ compiler is never named; the arXiv paper was read via its in-repo PDF copy.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C: the FastLZ README table has no methodology, but it points to lzbench, an independent third-party suite whose README (lzbench 2.4, public code, gcc 15.2.0, Makefile -O3 -DNDEBUG -fomit-frame-pointer -fstrict-aliasing, AMD EPYC 9555P single thread, silesia.tar) lists fastlz 0.5.0 against zlib 1.3.2 at -1/-6/-9.

corrections.baseline: zlib 1.3.2 (-1, -6, -9) in lzbench 2.4; zlib -1/-9 (version unstated) in the FastLZ README
corrections.claimed_speedup: lzbench 2.4 on silesia.tar, single thread AMD EPYC 9555P: fastlz 0.5.0 -1 273 MB/s compress, 587 MB/s decompress, ratio 49.37%; fastlz -2 294 / 561 MB/s, 47.61%; zlib 1.3.2 -1 89.0 / 297 MB/s, 36.45%; zlib -6 26.8 / 314 MB/s, 32.19%; zlib -9 11.3 / 318 MB/s, 31.92% (about 3.1x faster compression and 2.0x faster decompression than zlib -1, derived from page data). FastLZ README (enwik8, no methodology): FastLZ ratio 54.2%, 159 MB/s compress, 305 MB/s decompress; zlib -1 42.3%, 50 / 184 MB/s; zlib -9 36.5%, 11 / 185 MB/s. Ratio is compressed size as percent of input, so FastLZ output is larger.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: lzbench 2.4 release binary built with gcc 15.2.0; lzbench Makefile builds codecs with -O3 -DNDEBUG -fomit-frame-pointer -fstrict-aliasing; run options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4
corrections.hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04 (lzbench README); FastLZ README numbers have no hardware stated
corrections.stars_or_usage: 544 stars, 105 forks; included in lzbench; used in Godot, HHVM, Apache Traffic Server, Calligra, OSv, Netty, Death Stranding and as a basis for Blosc per README
corrections.caveats: FastLZ README table has no CPU, compiler, flags or lzbench version and appears to come from an old run; the lzbench 2.4 numbers are the reproducible ones. In the same lzbench table LZ4 1.10.0 (550 / 3832 MB/s at 47.60%), Snappy 1.3.1 and LZF 3.6 match or beat FastLZ, and zlib-ng 2.3.3 -1 (196 / 466 MB/s at 44.41%) narrows the gap to zlib-class codecs, so FastLZ is faster than stock zlib but not state of the art. Last release 0.5.0 dates from 2020; last commit 2024-08-02 (CI and warning fixes).

notes: Real, widely used entry; tier raised C to A via lzbench's independent, fully specified run (fastlz 0.5.0 row checked as this project's row). License MIT confirmed (LICENSE.MIT); last commit 2024-08-02 so 'stale' is correct.
